blocks.x: Sanctions screening rebuilt on a decision hub, screening latency down 84% and false positives down 47% without widening risk appetite

A cross-border payments group: Banking margins live between risk and speed: approve too slowly and the customer leaves, approve too fast and the losses follow. The Achala program started where that tension is sharpest —. The baseline signed in week two made the cost visible in units the finance team already owns, and the engagement ran under the standard Achala charter — a named metric, a named control owner and gates that evidence every move.

The baseline fortnight measured what the batch design actually cost: 41% of interbank transfers sat in manual screening queues longer than four hours, and correspondent partners had begun routing around the corridor at peak hours.

Every alert was treated as equal, a salary payment and a shell-company pattern hit the same queue. Screeners worked oldest-first, so the riskiest items waited behind the easiest ones, and the audit trail could not say why an item had been released.

We rebuilt screening as an event-driven decision hub: messages scored at ingest, a policy layer separating risk appetite from detection logic, and a workbench where alert dossiers assemble themselves, names, network links, prior dispositions, before a human opens them. Agents prepare; people decide; every release is replayable line by line.

blocks.x: The generalizable pieces here are the queue-ranking policy and the dossier assembly pattern, both moved to two other corridors with estate-specific rework. What did not transfer was the scorer; it had been trained on this group's own disposition history, and pretending otherwise would have been the expensive mistake.
